blocks.content: Docker accumulates disk usage quietly, old images, stopped containers, unused volumes, and build cache all pile up over time until a host unexpectedly runs low on space.
1. Seeing Where the Space Actually Went
blocks.text: 1. Seeing Where the Space Actually Went

blocks.content: docker system df breaks down exactly how much disk space images, containers, volumes, and build cache are each using, the essential first step before deciding what to clean up.

blocks.alt: A clear breakdown before deciding what to reclaim

blocks.content:
docker system df
# TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
# Images          42        6         8.1GB     6.3GB (77%)
# Containers      6         2         120MB     80MB (66%)
# Volumes         12        3         2.4GB     1.9GB (79%)
# Build Cache     84        0         3.2GB     3.2GB (100%)

code.content:
docker system df
# TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE

# Containers      6         2         120MB     80MB (66%)

codes.bash:
docker system df
# TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE

blocks.content: Every rebuild that changes a tag, or every pull of a new version, can leave the previous image sitting around as a "dangling" image, no longer tagged, no longer obviously in use, but still consuming disk space until explicitly cleaned up.

blocks.alt: Untagged, unused images pile up silently over time

blocks.content: 3. Build Cache Is a Common Surprise
blocks.text: 3. Build Cache Is a Common Surprise

blocks.content: BuildKit's build cache, covered in the Docker Build module, is genuinely valuable for build speed, but it also grows continuously as you build, and it is easy to forget it is even there, this is very often the single largest, least expected line item in docker system df.

blocks.alt: Often the largest, most surprising line item on a dev machine

blocks.content: docker system prune -a is the broadest cleanup command, it removes every stopped container, every unused network, every image not currently referenced by a running container, and (with --volumes) unused volumes and build cache too, genuinely effective, but worth pointing at deliberately rather than running blindly on a machine with something important sitting unused.

blocks.alt: A broad, effective cleanup, worth using deliberately

blocks.content:
docker system prune -a --volumes
# Removes unused containers, networks, images, volumes, and build cache

code.content:
docker system prune -a --volumes
# Removes unused containers, networks, images, volumes, and build cache

codes.bash:
docker system prune -a --volumes
# Removes unused containers, networks, images, volumes, and build cache

blocks.content: 5. Targeted Cleanup When You Know Exactly What to Remove
blocks.text: 5. Targeted Cleanup When You Know Exactly What to Remove

blocks.content: When you know specifically what is safe to remove, a narrower command is often the better choice than a broad prune, docker image prune for just dangling images, docker volume prune for just unused volumes, less risk of removing something you actually still needed.

blocks.alt: A precise cleanup, when you know exactly what you don't need anymore

blocks.content:
docker image prune       # just dangling, untagged images
docker volume prune      # just volumes no container references
docker builder prune     # just the build cache

code.content:
docker image prune       # just dangling, untagged images
docker volume prune      # just volumes no container references
docker builder prune     # just the build cache

codes.bash:
docker image prune       # just dangling, untagged images
docker volume prune      # just volumes no container references
docker builder prune     # just the build cache

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker system df shows exactly where disk space is going, images, containers, volumes, and build cache all accumulate quietly over time.
docker system prune -a is a broad, effective cleanup, targeted commands like image prune or volume prune are the safer choice when you know exactly what to remove.
